findings.title: Keyword-substring whitelist suppresses real weak passwords/passphrases
findings.detail: onlyNames() exempts a quoted "password or secret" value from the rule whenever it is letters-only, no digits, and either camelCase or joined by -/_/. AND lower.contains() finds any of ["secret","token","password","passwd","key","client","vault","entry","access","name","id"] anywhere in the string — a plain substring test, not tied to the key it's assigned to and not requiring the value to actually equal/represent that key's name. Tracing it: `apiKey = "production-access-key"` is a dash-joined, digit-free, lowercase value containing "access" and "key", so onlyNames returns true and breaks() suppresses it, even though this is a realistic, low-entropy secret someone could commit. Likewise a passphrase like `token = "wonderful-rapid-journey"` is suppressed because "rapid" contains the substring "id". This directly contradicts the change's own stated guarantee ("a weak password... and a passphrase... still count") and is a real regression in the scanner's core job of catching committed secrets. The added tests don't catch it because the chosen passphrase example (correct-horse-battery-staple) and the "still counts" cases were picked to avoid every keyword / include digits.

findings.title: Special-case dispatch keyed on a literal rule-name string
findings.detail: breaks() decides whether to apply onlyNames() filtering purely by comparing rule.name to the string literal "password or secret". `rules` is a plain `[(name: String, pattern: Regex<Substring>)]` array with nothing the compiler can check, so if that rule's name is ever edited (e.g. rewording the Finding text), breaks() silently falls back to the old `text.contains(rule.pattern)` path with no name-filtering at all, reintroducing the false positives this change fixes, with no compiler error and no test that would point at the cause.
